Q11012952.summary: At the center of a Roman floor mosaic in Dorset, the bust of a clean-shaven man with deep-set eyes appears before the Chi-Rho, the monogram of Christ's name, flanked by two pomegranates. Generally identified as Christ himself, it may be one of the oldest portraits of Jesus anywhere in the Roman Empire and is a remarkable witness to faith on the far northwestern frontier. Its frank, direct gaze gives a rare glimpse of how Christians at the edge of the Roman world imagined their Lord.
facts: The mosaic was discovered on 12 September 1963 by the local blacksmith, Walter John White, while digging foundations.
On stylistic grounds it is attributed to a mosaic workshop based at Durnovaria (modern Dorchester).
The adjoining panel shows the classical hero Bellerophon slaying the Chimera, often read in a Christian sense as good triumphing over evil.
It was chosen as Object 44 in the BBC Radio 4 series 'A History of the World in 100 Objects'.
Q11012952.notes: Dated on stylistic grounds to the 4th century (Wikipedia); excavations found nothing earlier than c. 270. The mosaic was lifted again and broken up in 1997, and only the central roundel is now displayed.

Q60755927.summary: Christ stands full-length and frontal, blessing with his right hand and holding a jewelled Gospel book, while the twelve apostles appear as busts, six in a column on each side, all turned toward him. With his large eyes fixed on the viewer and lips slightly parted, he seems about to send them out to preach the Gospel to the world. The plaque probably formed the centrepiece of a precious book cover, much like the book Christ himself carries.
facts: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates the plaque c. 970–980 and attributes it to Ottonian Milan.
Wikipedia notes that it is thought to come from the same workshop as the Magdeburg ivories, though it was probably always intended for a book binding.
Q60755927.notes: CMA 1967.65; 18.2 × 9.9 cm. Cleveland's culture string ('Ottonian, Italy, Milan, Gothic period, 10th century') contains an evident error ('Gothic'); place simplified to Milan.

cur:catacombs2-civita-castellana-sarcoph.summary: Seven niches framed by spiral columns hold biblical scenes on this fourth-century sarcophagus, now the high altar of the cathedral. Between Old Testament scenes at either end (Abraham's sacrifice and Daniel destroying the dragon), the five central niches show Christ foretelling Peter's denial, healing the paralytic, giving the keys to Peter, healing the woman with an issue of blood and changing water into wine at Cana.
facts: Italian Wikipedia identifies the seven scenes and describes the sarcophagus as one of the most valuable works in the cathedral.
Daniel destroying the dragon (from the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel) is a rarer subject than Daniel among the lions.
cur:catacombs2-civita-castellana-sarcoph.notes: Commons dates it '3rd–4th century'; the columnar type with these scenes belongs to the mid- to late 4th century.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-healing-leper.summary: Christ, labelled IHS XPS and followed by his apostles, stretches out his hand to a leper, labelled 'leprosus', who bends toward him, his body covered with spots. The clear, frieze-like composition is typical of the Reichenau painters.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.
cur:manuscripts-egberti-healing-leper.notes: A black-and-white version of the same miniature is on Commons as CodexEgberti-Fol021vCleansingOfTheLeper.jpg.

cur:monumental-san-saba-healing-paralyti.summary: Under a tiled roof supported by columns, the paralysed man on his bed is lowered on ropes into the room, while in the foreground Christ, haloed and in a dark robe, stands among the people; at the right the healed man walks away with his bed on his back. Two moments of the Gospel story are thus shown together, with Greek inscriptions above.
facts: The fragment comes from the earlier oratory discovered beneath the nave of the 12th-century basilica of San Saba during excavations in May 1900.
The religious community here goes back to about 645, when monks who had fled the monastery of Saint Sabas (Mar Saba) in Palestine settled on the Little Aventine after attending the Lateran Council.

cur:objects2-met-koimesis-icon.summary: Beneath a pierced arch with a beaded border, the Virgin lies on her bier surrounded by grieving apostles who bend over her head and feet. Behind the bier stands Christ, who holds his Mother's soul, shown as a small swaddled child, while angels descend with veiled hands to receive it. The ivory's crisp carving, deep undercutting and architectural frame are characteristic of the finest Constantinopolitan work of the late 10th century.
facts: The scene of the Koimesis reverses the familiar image of the Virgin holding the infant Christ: here Christ holds his Mother's soul as she once held him.
The plaque came to the Met as part of the J. Pierpont Morgan gift of 1917.

wga:zearly/2/2paintin/2mustair3.summary: In this red-ochre fresco, Christ, haloed and robed, steps forward and reaches out his hand to the mouth of a man who bows low before him, while apostles stand behind Christ and a group of onlookers watch from beneath an arch at the right. Though faded, the broad, rhythmic figures convey the moment of touch by which the silent man is healed. The scene belongs to the extensive Carolingian cycle of the life of Christ in the remote Alpine church of Müstair.
facts: The convent church of Saint John at Müstair, founded around 780 perhaps at Charlemagne's instigation, preserves the best-surviving cycle of Carolingian wall painting; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
The paintings were rediscovered in 1896 and fully uncovered by 1950; parts had been painted over in the 12th century.
The Web Gallery of Art places this scene on the north wall and suggests the painters were itinerant artists trained in a Byzantine-influenced Italian tradition.
wga:zearly/2/2paintin/2mustair3.notes: Title from the WGA. The specific miracle (deaf-mute of Mark 7 or the mute demoniac of Matthew 9:32–33) is not confirmed by a second source; Mark 7 is suggested because Christ touches the man's mouth. Müstair is in Switzerland, not Italy.

feat:sant-apollinare-in-classe-transfigu.summary: Rather than a human figure, the apse presents the Transfiguration through symbols: a great jewelled cross set in a starry blue disc, with a tiny bust of Christ at its centre, flanked by Moses and Elijah, while three sheep below stand for Peter, James and John. Beneath, Saint Apollinaris, Ravenna's first bishop, prays among his flock in a green paradise of trees and flowers. It is a subtle and luminous image of Christ's hidden glory revealed through the cross.
facts: Above the cross is the Greek word IXΘYC ('fish'), an acrostic for 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour'; below it is the Latin 'SALUS MUNDI', 'Salvation of the world'.
The hand of God emerges from the clouds at the top, recalling the voice from heaven at the Transfiguration.
The basilica was consecrated in 549 by Archbishop Maximian, the same bishop whose ivory throne survives in Ravenna.
It is one of eight early Christian monuments of Ravenna inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
